sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Most world models for future prediction prioritize aestetic quality of generated videos, but offer only weak physical grounding and limited geometric consistency over time, due to the lack of explicit 4D modeling. In this paper, we introduce plan4d, a possible next milestone towards building a generative plannable 4D world model that predicts future RGB videos together with dense 4D geometry, including depth, cameras, point clouds, and scene flow from an observed scene context and text-specified actions. Since training data with paired actions and dense 4D annotations is inherently scarce, plan4d leverages the complementary priors of foundational video generators and 3D reconstructors. Specifically, we propose a model-stitching architecture that couples Depth Anything 3 with LongCat-Video and augments it with an auxiliary DPT head for scene-flow prediction. The resulting model allows us to plan and generate complex, long-horizon, and fine-grained actions in a dynamic 3D scenes, while substantially improving both visual fidelity and geometric accuracy of the generated future videos. Extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that plan4d achieves state-of-the-art performance in generative 4D modeling of environmental reactions. Project Page: https://fogradio.github.io/plan4d-project

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Given an observed scene context and set of text-specified actions, we consider the task of generative plannable 4D worlds, new paradigm for predicting reliable futures for the physical world that jointly produces visually plausible RGB frames and physically grounded 4D geometry including depth, camera dynamics, and scene flow within single feed-forward model. Prior observation-prediction models formulate future prediction largely as RGB synthesis [25, 86], often on per-frame basis, notably UniSim [106], Genie 13 [13, 76, 8], NWM [10], and V-JEPA 2 [4]. By contrast, with our actionable 4D future world model, humans and AI agents can plan and execute complex, long-horizon, and fine-grained actions in the explicit 3D environment, such as picking up cup, opening bottle, or navigating through cluttered room. These dynamic 3D quantities are essential for accurate measurement, reliable simulation, and effective execution of downstream tasks [54, 24, 59, 41, 33]. major bottleneck of this task is the lack of suitable datasets, namely action-conditioned video sequences paired with rich text and comprehensive 3D annotations, including camera trajectories, accurate dense depth and motion. For example, large-scale video-caption datasets [7, 98, 18] may still lack detailed captions for physical fine-grained actions; the latest Action-100M [15] dataset provides detailed action annotations but without 3D annotations, while most dynamic 3D datasets [31, 30, 51] are relatively small in scale or lack natural actions. Correspondingly, powerful baselines have emerged in parallel on these separate data sources, including video generators [35, 12, 11, 81, 34, 53, 108, 90, 66, 87], action-conditioned world models [106, 13, 76, 8, 10, 4, 48, 58], and 3D reconstructors [97, 57, 96, 92, 52, 99, 64, 114]. Despite being trained to build the same physical world, these models still operate as isolated systems for particular tasks. Standard pixel-level generators excel at synthesizing visually realistic RGB frames [102], but typically lack physical consistency [101, 61]; and 3D models recover explicit geometry well [94] but are largely reconstruction-centric and static. Even advanced 4D frameworks [116, 47, 82, 121, 50, 73, 72, 55] only infer motion from observed frames and cannot generate action-conditioned future worlds. As result, none of these families alone provides generative plannable 4D world, in which appearance, geometry, camera and action-conditioned future dynamics evolve consistently over time. What if, given these different dataset sources, we stitch them together to model the same underlying 4D world? To achieve such generative plannable 4D world, we propose PLAN4D, unified framework for planning and generating dense 4D worlds from observed context and action descriptions. Our core insight is to decouple the acquisition of strong geometric priors from the generation of future dynamics, then reconnect them through stitched latent world model that jointly plans RGB appearance and dense 4D geometry, unlike recent methods [85, 117, 22, 71, 27] that attempt to learn 4D world models geometry from scratch. Such paradigm reduces the tasks learning difficulty and data requirements, while allowing us to leverage the powerful priors of pretrained video generators and 3D reconstructors to achieve complex, long-horizon and fine-grained dynamics. In practice, this paradigm requires solving several coupled challenges. i) the model must extend frozen 3D foundation model from static scenes to dynamic 4D prediction while preserving its geometric consistency. ii) it must align geometry tokens with the latent space of video generator without destroying the pretrained generative prior. iii) it must learn from real, unlabeled action videos without dense 4D supervision [112]. iv) it must also ensure consistency across the generated RGB, depth, camera, point clouds, and scene flow. Recent methods, including VIST3A [29], Geometry Forcing [100], and Gen3R [37], couple 3D reconstructors with video generators for static text-to-3D or scene-level 3D generation. We extend this direction to full actionable 4D world generation, jointly predicting full 4D geometry and appearance in future video sequences depicting fine-grained actions. Unlike prior approaches that use geometry mainly as an auxiliary constraint [100, 6, 110, 26, 3], or decode geometry only after RGB generation [24], our PLAN4D turns video generator into an actionable 4D world model, which explicitly aligns future appearance and 4D structure inside the shared evolving video latent state. To preserve strong geometric priors while extending them beyond reconstruction, we augment Depth Anything 3 [64] (DA3) with lightweight token-only scene-flow head that predicts dense forward 3D motion from intermediate geometry tokens, while keeping its pretrained depth and camera-ray predictions intact. To connect this geometric readout with future generation, we learn latent-to-geometry stitching module that maps video VAE latents into selected DA3 block and trains it with token distillation and geometric supervision. The resulting stitched 2 decoder provides stable, differentiable interface from video latents to full 4D geometry. We then train the video generator against this frozen geometric interface, so unlabeled action videos can supervise not only visual prediction but also physically grounded 4D consistency. At inference time, single generated latent future yields RGB frames and dense 4D geometry in one feed-forward pass. Our main contributions can be summarized as follows: We take step towards the new paradigm of generative plannable 4D worlds, which jointly generates future RGB appearance and corresponding full 4D geometry, including depth, camera rays, point clouds, and scene flow, from observed context and action descriptions. We propose PLAN4D, unified framework with scene-flow head and geometry-video stitching mechanism that connect frozen 3D foundation model with pretrained video generator, preserving geometric priors while enabling action-conditioned dynamic 4D future prediction from unlabeled videos. We illustrate how PLAN4D can achieve state-of-the-art performance in dense 4D world generation, improving both visual realism and geometric accuracy across scene flow, 3D reconstruction, and action-conditioned video prediction through extensive experiments.

sections.title: 2 Related Works
sections.content: 4D world models. Recent work has begun to model 4D worlds from two complementary directions. Explicit dynamics methods such as ParticleFormer [40] and PointWorld [41] predict particle trajectories or point-level motion, but mainly operate in structured 3D state spaces rather than generating rich future 4D. 4D-native generative models instead learn spatiotemporal world evolution, ranging from dynamic reconstruction, visual planning, and image-to-4D generation in Aether [85] and 4DNeX [21], to RGB-D or geometry-aware scene generation in TesserAct [117] and Robo4DGen [69]. GWM [70], iMoWM [113], and Kinema4D [105] further explore Gaussian, tokenized, and kinematics-driven representations, while FantasyWorld [22], WorldReel [27], TeleWorld [20], HY-World 2.0 [43], and Lyra 2.0 [80] couple video generation with geometric prediction for more unified world modeling. Despite this progress, existing systems typically emphasize either explicit geometric forecasting or large-scale generative simulation, and they rarely integrate the complementary priors of pretrained geometry foundation models into the latent dynamics of video generation. Aligning 3D Reconstruction and Video Generation. Early uses of generative priors for 3D synthesis mostly follow cascade, where geometric constraints are applied to generated outputs rather than to internal generative states [77, 28, 95]. Later methods tighten this link through reconstruction-guided diffusion or distillation, as in GenFusion [103], VideoScene [91], and Lyra [5]. Recent work moves the alignment into feature or latent spaces. Geometry Forcing [100] aligns intermediate diffusion features with pretrained geometric representations [111], Gen3R [37] aligns geometry and appearance latents for joint generation, and GLD [46] repurposes geometric features as multi-view diffusion latents. From the model-stitching view [56, 9], VIST3A [29] connects pretrained video VAE with 3D network at linearly matchable layers. Our method builds on this direction, but stitches video diffusion model to 3D foundation model so that RGB synthesis and dense 4D geometry can be optimized and decoded from shared latent rollout.

During joint training, the stitched decoder is frozen and acts as differentiable geometry critic for the video generator; at inference time, RGB video and dense 4D structure are decoded from the shared latent trajectory. We parametrize fθ with model-stitching architecture that couples video generator, LongCatVideo [87] (which uses the Wan 2.1 VAE [90]), with foundational 3D reconstructor, Depth Anything 3 [64] (DA3). The key insight is that, by building on the pretrained video generator and 3D reconstructor, our model can leverage the complementary priors of these two foundational models to achieve both high visual fidelity and strong geometric consistency in the generated future videos, unlike training it from scratch [85, 117, 22, 27], which is extremely challenging and data-hungry. To improve the motion modeling capability of DA3, we first augment it with an auxiliary DPT-style scene flow head in section 3.1. In section 3.2, we then stitch the video generator and the augmented DA3 together through learnable latent-to-geometry stitching module, followed by distillation and geometric supervision process to calibrate the stitched model in section 3.3. Finally, we train the joint model in section 3.4. 3.1 Augmenting DA3 for Dynamic Scene Flow Prediction The physical world is not collection of independent per-frame geometries. To model the dynamics and correspondence of the 4D world, we augment DA3 [64] with dense scene flow head that predicts the 3D motion of each pixel. Following the original DPT-style decoder in DA3, the new head ingests the four intermediate token maps of the frozen encoder, and outputs dense three-channel motion field via lightweight prediction layer. Note that, the original encoder, as well as the depth and camera pose branches, remains unchanged; we simply add dedicated motion branch. Our analysis in Section shows that frozen DA3 tokens already encode cross-frame motion cues, which supports using this branch as lightweight readout rather than full motion model. In particular, for each frame t, the new head predicts scene flow on the pixel lattice of that frame. Each valid pixel stores the forward 3D displacement from time to + 1. We apply only rotation because scene flow is vector quantity rather than 3D point. This representation keeps spatial indexing local to each frame while expressing all motion vectors in temporally stable basis. As result, the predicted dynamics remain consistent under camera motion and align naturally with the depth, ray, and point-based geometry produced by DA3. sections.title: 4 Experiments
sections.content: 4.1 Experimental Settings. Implementation. PLAN4D is trained in three stages on diverse datasets due to the lack of large-scale data with paired action and dense 4D annotations. (1) We train the designed scene-flow head on top of frozen DA3 using PointOdyssey [118], Dynamic Replica [49], Virtual KITTI 2 [14], BlinkVision [62], and OmniWorld-Game [119] for 20 epochs on 16 H100 GPUs. (2) We fit the latent-to-geometry stitching module on small subset of the above datasets to initialize the interface from Wan latents to DA3 tokens. Then we finetune the stitched decoder with the scene-flow-head data mixture augmented by ScanNet++ [109] and MVS-Synth [39]. This stage uses 64 H20 GPUs and runs one hybrid epoch over the full data mixture, where the same mixed sampling schedule is traversed once with ground-truth geometric supervision and once with teacher-student distillation. When ground-truthsupervised sample does not provide scene-flow annotations, we set its scene-flow loss to zero. (3) We finally train the DiT on subset of Action100M [15] for one epoch using 64 H20 GPUs. All stages use per-GPU batch size of 1. Additional dataset details, optimization details, losses, and supervision definitions are provided in Section B. Evaluation. We evaluate PLAN4D along three axes that correspond to its intended use as generative 4D world model. (1) we evaluate dynamic 4D geometry through scene flow on MOViF [31], Dynamic Replica, and PointOdyssey using 81-frame clips, and report endpoint error together with AP D0.05 against reconstruction and motion baselines. (2) we test whether the stitched decoder preserves DA3 geometry after replacing the RGB encoder with Wan-latent input pathway. This evaluation covers reconstruction, camera, and depth benchmarks, including ETH3D [79], ScanNet++, Dynamic Replica, Dynamic-RE10K [19], MOVi-F, and RobbySimVal [83], with comparisons to RGBbased 3D foundation models and latent-to-geometry baselines. To further assess in-the-wild generalization, we additionally sample 100 five-second clips from Epic-Kitchens100 [23], which contains everyday human-object interactions in kitchen environments, and evaluate all compared methods under the same joint-generation protocol. These benchmarks test whether single generated rollout can jointly preserve visual quality [65, 120], action-text alignment [16], and temporally coherent 4D structure. We report video quality and instruction following with VBench-style video metrics and video-caption similarity [42]. For depth, reconstruction, and camera estimation, we follow the same protocol as the stitched-decoder evaluation. We compare with recent 4D world-generation and geometry-generation baselines, including VIST3A [29], TesserAct [117], and Gen3R [37], on the modalities each method supports. 4.2 Main Results Scene Flow Estimation. We first test whether frozen DA3 geometry prior can support dynamic 4D motion prediction beyond static reconstruction. This is stringent setting because scene flow requires temporally coherent geometry rather than accurate per-frame depth alone. Table 1 shows that both scene-flow variants remain competitive on all three benchmarks while using the smallest training set among the compared methods. The RGB-based DA3 variant is particularly strong on the harder real dynamic benchmarks, suggesting that frozen DA3 tokens already support reliable dense 4D motion readout. The stitched variant performs best on the controlled synthetic benchmark and remains near the top on Dynamic Replica, which matters because it is the decoder interface used during joint video training. The qualitative results in Figure 3 show cleaner boundaries, more stable articulated motion, and better global 3D structure than the baselines. Overall, these results validate the first step of PLAN4D: DA3 can be extended from geometry reconstruction to strong dynamic 4D readout, and this capability largely survives the latent-to-geometry stitching step. sections.title: 5 Conclusion
sections.content: We introduce the problem of generative plannable 4D worlds, where model must generate future scenes with rich 4D attributes, including RGB appearance, depth, camera poses, point clouds, and scene flow, from observed context and action descriptions. To this end, we propose PLAN4D, unified framework that decouples the acquisition of strong geometric priors from the generation of future dynamics, then reconnects them through stitched latent world model. By augmenting frozen DA3 with token-only scene-flow head and learning latent-to-geometry stitching interface from video VAE latents to geometry tokens, PLAN4D turns pretrained video generator into an actionable 4D world model whose RGB, depth, camera rays, point clouds, and scene flow are read out from the same evolving latent state in single feed-forward pass. Experiments show that this design preserves strong geometric behavior while improving dense 4D world generation across scene flow, reconstruction, and action-conditioned future prediction, without requiring manual 4D annotations for action videos. We hope this perspective helps move future world modeling beyond video-only prediction toward unified, measurable, and plannable 4D world models.

Frozen DA3 Tokens Already Encode Cross-Frame Motion Cues The lightweight DPT scene flow head above is only useful if the frozen DA3 encoder tokens already preserve motion-relevant structure. The central question of this section is therefore simple: before any scene-flow supervision reaches the decoder, do frozen DA3 tokens already know which location in frame + 1 corresponds to location in frame t? If the answer is yes, then shallow head can decode dense motion by reading out representation that already contains cross-frame geometry and correspondence cues. If the answer is no, then good scene-flow predictions would have to come from the capacity of the head alone. To make this question concrete, let zt(p) denote the frozen DA3 token at spatial cell in frame t. Point Odyssey [118] provides ground-truth tracks, which let us identify the corresponding target cell p+ in frame + 1 for each valid source cell p. We then probe the token space without using the scene flow head. Our analysis uses the Point Odyssey test split with 128 clips from 5 scenes. All values in Table 5 are weighted over clips by the number of valid token pairs or valid flow tokens. Figure 7 aggregates all 6,132,636 positive pairs, 6,132,636 negative pairs, and 2,160,723 token-difference vectors. We use four complementary probes, each answering different question about the frozen representation. The first probe is correspondence similarity [84]. It asks whether token is more similar to its true match than to an unrelated token from the next frame: spos = cos(cid:0)zt(p), zt+1(p+)(cid:1), sneg = cos(cid:0)zt(p), zt+1(q)(cid:1), (6) where is random negative sampled from frame + 1. This is the cleanest test of whether correspondence information is present [44]. If frozen DA3 tokens contain motion-relevant structure, the spos distribution should shift to the right of the sneg distribution. The margin = spos sneg and the probability Pr(spos > sneg) summarize how reliably the two distributions separate. The second probe is token retrieval [74]. Instead of comparing one positive and one negative, we search over all target tokens in frame + 1: ˆp = arg max qPt+1 cos(cid:0)zt(p), zt+1(q)(cid:1). (7) This is stronger operational test. It asks whether nearest-neighbor search in frozen token space can recover the correct destination cell. We report Top-1 exact, which measures whether the retrieved cell is exactly the ground-truth cell, and PCK@1 and PCK@3, which measure whether retrieval falls within 1 or 3 token cells of the ground-truth location [107]. High retrieval accuracy means that the token space is not only separable on average, but also organized enough to support direct correspondence lookup. The third probe is token-flow readout. After retrieval returns ˆp, we interpret it as token-level motion estimate ˆd = ˆp and compare it with the ground-truth token displacement. This probe is more demanding than similarity or retrieval because it asks single nearest-neighbor lookup to act as motion predictor. The resulting endpoint error and direction cosine should be interpreted as evidence for how directly motion can be read out from the frozen tokens without learned decoder [104]. The fourth probe is PCA on token differences. For each matched pair, we form zt(p) = zt+1(p+) zt(p). (8) We then perform PCA on these token differences [78]. This analysis does not test whether motion is present at all. The earlier probes already answer that question more directly. Instead, PCA asks more specific question: is the motion signal concentrated in small linear subspace, or is it distributed across many token dimensions? If the first few principal components explain most of the variance, then motion could be close to linearly disentangled [2]. If the variance remains spread out, then motion is still present, but encoded in more distributed form. This distinction matters for interpreting the role of the DPT head. low-dimensional linear code would be easy to read out with almost any linear probe, while distributed code benefits from structured multiscale decoding. Before discussing the numbers, it is useful to clarify how they should be interpreted. Similarity and retrieval are the strongest probes in this section because they make the fewest modeling assumptions. They only ask whether true cross-frame matches are already nearby in frozen token space. Token flow is harder probe because it asks nearest-neighbor retrieval to behave like motion estimator. 19 Figure 7: Aggregated token-space evidence on the Point Odyssey test split. Left: cosine similarity distributions computed from frozen DA3 tokens. Right: explained variance of the top principal components of token differences zt = zt+1 zt, aggregated over all test clips. Similarity measures token-level separability between true matches and negatives. Retrieval measures whether nearest-neighbor search recovers the correct target cell. Token flow measures how well that retrieval can be turned into direct motion estimate. PCA measures whether motion is concentrated in small linear subspace. It only means that the information is not cleanly isolated in the top principal components. Figure 7 and Table 5 provide direct evidence that frozen DA3 tokens preserve cross-frame correspondence structure. The similarity distributions are cleanly separated, with ground-truth matches consistently closer in token space than random negatives. Nearest-neighbor retrieval leads to the same conclusion under stronger all-candidates test. These two probes show that, even without any learned motion decoder, the frozen representation already places true future matches near the source token and usually retrieves target very close to the correct location. The token-flow probe refines this picture. simple nearest-neighbor displacement readout already recovers meaningful motion, which indicates that the frozen tokens encode where points are likely to move. At the same time, this probe is weaker than similarity and retrieval, which suggests that the motion signal is not exposed as trivial one-step velocity code. This is precisely where structured decoder becomes useful. Our DPT head can pool multiscale context and impose spatial coherence to transform this latent correspondence signal into dense scene flow. The PCA results should be read as auxiliary evidence. The dominant components explain only limited portion of the token-difference variance, and their alignment with flow magnitude remains weak. This does not argue against motion information in the frozen tokens. Instead, PCA indicates that motion is encoded in distributed high-dimensional form rather than concentrated in single linear direction. 20 Table 6: Stage-wise training datasets for the 81-frame PLAN4D pipeline. Frozen DA3 encoder tokens already contain scene-flow-relevant information, especially in the form of cross-frame correspondence structure. The strongest evidence comes from the probes that require almost no decoder assumptions, namely similarity separation and nearest-neighbor retrieval. The weaker token-flow and PCA probes refine this picture. They suggest that the motion signal is real, but distributed and not trivially linearized. Our DPT head succeeds because it decodes and regularizes this latent signal into dense metric predictions. In other words, the scene flow branch acts as an informed readout of the pretrained geometry representation, rather than separate module that has to create motion information from scratch.

sections.title: B Training Details
sections.content: B.1 Dataset and Optimization Summary All dataset statistics in this paper correspond to the 81-frame manifests. Every manifest row therefore satisfies the temporal constraint = 4k + 1 with = 81. Table 6 summarizes the stage-wise training data. Stage 1 trains only the DA3 scene-flow readout. Stage 2 finetunes the stitched decoder with hybrid ground-truth and teacher-student supervision. Stage 3 optimizes the action-conditioned video model, where Action100M contributes text-conditioned video clips without paired 4D labels. Stage 1 mixes 11,956 training clips from five dynamic datasets. The sampler uses dataset-wise mixture weights of 1.0 together with size-aware mixing exponent α = 0.5, which interpolates between uniform-over-datasets and proportional-to-size sampling. The stage-1 manifest directory also contains held-out or diagnostic subsets such as PointOdyssey test, PointOdyssey sample, and Dynamic Replica valid clips for validation and smoke tests. Stage 2 contains 122,225 GT-capable training clips. Among them, 13,521 clips expose scene-flow labels, while the remaining 108,704 clips provide only depth, ray, camera, and point-cloud supervision. In hybrid decoder training, we build separate GT and distill dataloaders from the same manifest list and randomly shuffle the union of GT and distill steps once per epoch. This realizes one GT pass and one distillation pass over the full mixture in single hybrid epoch. The stage-3 Action100M subset is constructed in two steps. We first start from the filtered 81-frame TI2V manifest action100m_train_ti2v_81f.filtered.jsonl, whose rows already satisfy task_type=ti2v, cond_frames=1, and num_frames=81. We then score the corresponding clip-level entries from action100m_clip_index_81f.filtered.jsonl and keep only clips that pass high-precision action-quality filter. The clip-level decision uses fields such as 21 prompt_action, level, and node_duration_sec. We drop clips with node duration shorter than 1.6 seconds, hierarchy depth above 10, missing action text, action text identical to the generic description, action text shorter than four words, prompt patterns dominated by on-screen text or audio-style narration, uncertain descriptions, or generic action stubs. The retained manifest action100m_train_ti2v_81f.action_hq.keep.jsonl contains 249,422 clips, which is 28.6% of the 871,785 filtered TI2V rows. Because Action100M does not provide paired 4D geometry, these clips are used only in the distillation branch during stage 3. Per-dataset roles. PointOdyssey provides articulated outdoor motion with sparse track supervision that we rasterize into dense forward scene flow, which makes it particularly useful for supervising correspondence-aware motion. Dynamic Replica contributes denser dynamic stereo geometry with strong camera and scene-flow signals. BlinkVision, Virtual KITTI 2, and OmniWorld broaden the synthetic motion distribution across indoor scenes, driving scenes, and open-world gameplay trajectories. ScanNet++ and MVS-Synth do not provide scene flow in our 81-frame setup, but they substantially enrich multiview depth, camera, and point-cloud supervision during stitched-decoder finetuning. Action100M serves different purpose from the geometry datasets. It injects large-scale action-conditioned video semantics into the joint model while relying on the frozen DA3 teacher for geometric targets. Evaluation datasets. We report three groups of held-out evaluations. For dynamic 4D motion, we evaluate on MOVi-F, Dynamic Replica, and PointOdyssey using 81-frame clips. MOVi-F tests controlled synthetic object motion, Dynamic Replica tests realistic dynamic stereo scenes, and PointOdyssey emphasizes articulated motion with long temporal support. For stitched-decoder geometry preservation, we evaluate on ETH3D, ScanNet++, Dynamic Replica, Dynamic-RE10K, MOVi-F, and RobbySimVal. These datasets cover static reconstruction, indoor multiview geometry, dynamic camera estimation, and robot-centric depth prediction. For action-conditioned world generation, we evaluate on RLBench with 210 samples, HOIGen-1M with 200 samples, Dynamic Replica with 480 samples, and PointOdyssey with 375 samples, which together span manipulation, hand-object interaction, and general dynamic-scene futures. We additionally evaluate 100 five-second Epic-Kitchens-100 clips to assess in-the-wild generalization to everyday human-object interactions in kitchen environments. This evaluation complements HoiGen with second real-world human-object interaction benchmark. Stage-3 comparison scope. We exclude several recent world-generation systems from the stage-3 comparison because they assume additional control inputs beyond the setting targeted in this paper. PointWorld requires depth input [41]. FantasyWorld, HY-World 2.0, Lyra 2.0, Geometry Forcing, and TeleWorld rely on trajectory-level control signals [22, 43, 80, 100, 20]. Kinema4D further requires robot-action kinematic representations [105]. These methods therefore do not match the task of predicting future RGB video together with dense 4D geometry from only an observed scene context and text-specified action, so we do not include them in the stage-3 comparison. Evaluation protocol and metric definitions. We follow the same three-way evaluation split as in the main paper and expand the scoring protocol here. Scene flow. We score only valid moving pixels indicated by the deformation mask. Predictions are first rescaled to the target point-map scale of each clip. When model predicts relative flow, we restore the target scale with the clip-level scene-flow scale before metric computation. If benchmark provides native-resolution labels, we resize predictions to that evaluation resolution before scoring. RLBench and HOIGen1M use their native action annotations, while Dynamic Replica and PointOdyssey do not provide action-level text in our stage-3 evaluation split, so we generate per-clip action captions with QwenVL-30B-Thinking and use them as the conditioning text for all compared methods. When baseline exposes compatible geometry output, we score its generated 4D structure with the same geometry protocol described above. 23 Epic-Kitchens-100 evaluation setting. We sample 100 clips, each five seconds long, and follow the same action-conditioned joint 4D generation protocol as the original comparison. Each method receives the initial RGB frame and an action description. We compare PLAN4D, TesserAct, Gen3R, and VIST3A using the same metric definitions and alignment procedures. The full evaluation reports six video metrics, namely subject consistency (SC), background consistency (BC), aesthetic quality (AQ), image quality (IQ), motion smoothness (MS), and video-caption similarity (Cap.Sim). Geometry is evaluated with depth AbsRel, δ1, δ2, and Chamfer-L1, together with camera RPE-R, RRA@10, and RRA@5. Higher scores are better except for AbsRel, Chamfer-L1, and RPE-R. The complete results appear in Table 8, and Table 3 retains six representative metrics for comparison with the other benchmarks. Stage-wise optimization details. For stage 1, the 81-frame manifest configuration uses AdamW with learning rate 105, weight decay 102, β = (0.9, 0.999), 100 warmup steps, gradient accumulation 2, and bf16 mixed precision. Inputs are resized to 504 504 with upper-bound resizing, the clip overlap is 1 frame, and the scene-flow loss adds zero-last-frame penalty with weight 0.1. sections.content: C.1 Ablation of the Joint Training Objective We ablate the final joint-training objective and evaluate each variant on HoiGen and Dynamic Replica under the action-conditioned world-generation protocol in Section 4.1. Each test example provides an initial RGB frame and an action description. HoiGen uses its native action annotations, while Dynamic Replica uses the per-clip action captions from the main evaluation. Each variant produces RGB video and dense geometry from its predicted latent trajectory using the frozen stitched decoder described in Section B.5. The variants isolate the terms of Equation (5). Only-RGB-Loss optimizes the latent flow-matching loss LFM without the geometry term. Only-Geo-Loss optimizes the weighted geometric loss λgeoLgeo without the flow-matching term. Ours (Full) combines both losses to train the video generator while keeping the stitched geometry decoder frozen. When geometric supervision is used, its targets come from the frozen DA3 teacher described in Section B.5. For both datasets, we report subject consistency, background consistency, depth AbsRel, depth δ1, and camera rotation RPER in Table 4. Higher consistency scores and δ1 are better, while lower AbsRel and RPER are better. Depth uses per-clip scale-shift alignment, and camera evaluation uses the same first-camera alignment and relative-rotation protocol as the main joint-generation comparison. On Dynamic Replica, the full objective achieves the best result on all five metrics. Compared with RGB-only training, subject and background consistency increase from 0.8998 and 0.9321 to 0.9356 and 0.9496. Depth AbsRel decreases from 0.0874 to 0.0696, δ1 increases from 0.9169 to 0.9306, and camera RPER decreases from 0.2615 to 0.1550. Geometry-only training performs worse on all reported metrics than both RGB-only training and the full objective, indicating that geometric supervision alone does not preserve visual consistency or ensure accurate geometry on this benchmark. The HoiGen results reveal different depth tradeoff. Geometry-only training attains the best depth scores, but weakens subject and background consistency and has higher camera rotation error than the full objective. Across both datasets, the full model gives the best subject and background consistency and camera estimates. These results support the complementary roles of the two losses: flow matching preserves action-conditioned visual quality, while geometric supervision regularizes the shared future latent state toward consistent depth and camera structure. C.3 Ablation for Stitched Decoder Finetuning Strategy The stitched decoder is trained for specific role. It must accept Wan VAE latents as input while retaining the geometric behavior of the original DA3 model. This creates tension between adaptation and preservation. Teacher-student distillation keeps the student close to the pretrained DA3 function, while ground-truth geometric supervision anchors the predictions to metric depth, camera, pointcloud, and motion annotations when such labels are available. We ablate this finetuning strategy to identify which ingredients are needed for stable latent-to-geometry decoder. We follow the same benchmarks and metrics as the main stitched-model evaluation in Table 2. The variants isolate the main design choices in the finetuning stage. Distillation only trains the student only from the frozen DA3 teacher outputs. The teacher receives the ground-truth RGB clip, and the student receives the Wan latent of the same clip. Distillation with feature loss introduces an auxiliary feature-matching term to regularize the stitched DA3 representation. Specifically, it applies an L1 penalty between the output features of the stitching layer and the corresponding block features from the teacher model. This constraint forces the projected latent tokens to remain aligned with the teachers feature manifold prior to dense decoding. GT supervision only removes the teacher and trains only from available dataset annotations. No scene-flow head keeps the depth, ray, camera, and reconstruction objectives but removes the motion branch during stitched-decoder finetuning. LoRA adaptation replaces the full update of the stitched decoder with parameter-efficient alternative [36] on the adapted DA3 computation path. Specifically, we apply low-rank update with both the rank and scaling factor α set to 32 and maintain learning rate of 1 104. The results show that output distillation alone is not enough. It preserves coarse camera behavior relatively well, but its reconstruction quality degrades noticeably. This suggests that matching final teacher predictions can transfer some global geometric structure, yet it does not fully constrain the accurate geometry after the RGB encoder has been replaced by latent input pathway. Compared to our full model trained with mixed supervision, combining output-space distillation and ground-truth data, incorporating an additional feature loss actually degrades performance. This phenomenon aligns with the insights of Huang et al. [38]. It suggests that rigid representation alignment cannot independently recover all the geometric behaviors required by the stitched decoder. Furthermore, enforcing such strict alignment may impair the flexibility of the learned representations since the underlying model architecture has changed. The GT-only variant fails for distinct reason. While direct supervision provides explicit targets, it eliminates the pretrained DA3 teacher signal that contains broad reconstruction priors. Furthermore, 30 some low quality ground-truth data can be sparse or inaccurate locally, hindering the transfer learning capabilities of the model. This observation aligns with the insights of Lin et al. [64]. Consequently, the network becomes highly sensitive to dataset coverage, annotation quality, and task imbalances. This vulnerability is particularly detrimental to camera estimation, where the teacher provides strong geometric prior that is exceedingly difficult to learn from supervised labels alone. These results clarify the proper role of ground-truth supervision within our system. It serves as valuable corrective signal but must complement distillation rather than replace it. The architectural and adaptation ablations further clarify what the finetuning stage must optimize. Removing the scene-flow head weakens both reported axes, even though the compact table does not directly score scene flow. This indicates that motion supervision contributes useful temporal pressure to the shared decoder representation and benefits the geometry heads beyond the motion output itself. LoRA adaptation is also insufficient for this transfer. It keeps some camera behavior, but reconstruction degrades severely, which suggests that the distribution shift from RGB tokens to Wan latents is too large for narrow low-rank update. The full model is strongest on both reported axes. Its advantage is most visible in reconstruction, where combining distillation and ground-truth supervision best preserves 3D structure under the latent input path. The camera gains are more modest because several variants already retain coarse camera cues, but the full objective still gives the most stable result. This ablation supports the hybrid finetuning strategy used in PLAN4D. Distillation preserves the broad DA3 prior, ground-truth geometry corrects metric errors left by teacher-only learning, and scene-flow supervision helps maintain temporal structure in the shared decoder features.

sections.title: D Limitations
sections.content: Our method serves as geometry-aware intermediate world model for predicting future visual and 4D geometric states, rather than an end-to-end embodied agent. Because it lacks closed-loop physical deployment and relies purely on offline benchmarks, the impact of prediction error accumulation on downstream decision-making remains untested. Future work must therefore integrate this predictive representation with explicit action policies to evaluate task success under real-world execution constraints.

sections.title: E Broader Impact
sections.content: While our geometry-aware world model advances embodied planning and simulation through structured 4D future predictions, it introduces potential risks, including misuse in surveillance and overreliance in safety-critical applications susceptible to prediction errors and data biases. To ensure responsible deployment, these predictive outputs must be treated as probabilistic forecasts requiring uncertainty-aware downstream validation, augmented with strict task-specific safeguards prior to physical execution, and rigorously evaluated against distribution shifts and embodied failure modes. These measures support more responsible use of geometry-aware world models.

sections.content: Sec. 4 and Appendix report GPU types (H100 80GB for Stage 1, H20 96GB for Stages 2 and 3), GPU counts (16 for Stage 1, 64 for Stages 2 and 3), per-GPU batch size (1), and training epochs for all three stages. Stage 1 takes approximately 60 hours on 16 H100 GPUs (960 H100 GPU hours); Stage 2 takes approximately 90 hours on 64 H20 GPUs (5,760 H20 GPU hours); Stage 3 takes approximately 160 hours on 64 H20 GPUs (10,240 H20 GPU hours), totaling approximately 16,960 GPU hours across all three stages. Inference runs on 8 H20 GPUs and takes approximately 15 minutes per clip. The full research project required additional compute beyond the reported training runs. Ablation studies on stitching adapter architectures and stitched-decoder finetuning strategies follow the same stage-wise GPU configuration and duration as the corresponding main experiments, contributing an estimated 34,000 additional GPU hours in total across all ablation variants.

sections.title: I More Experimental Results
sections.content: Full quantitative comparison. Table 8 reports the complete joint 4D generation evaluation across HoiGen, Epic-Kitchens-100, Dynamic Replica, PointOdyssey, and RLBench. Epic-Kitchens-100 extends this evaluation to everyday kitchen interactions under the same protocol, where PLAN4D achieves the best values on 10 of the 13 metrics. We group the metrics into video quality, depth and reconstruction, and camera estimation. The discussion below focuses only on metrics that are reported for the corresponding methods. Across video-quality metrics, PLAN4D achieves the best subject consistency on all five benchmarks and the best motion smoothness on HoiGen, Dynamic Replica, and RLBench. It leads in caption similarity on Epic-Kitchens-100 and PointOdyssey, while VIST3A leads on HoiGen, Dynamic Replica, and RLBench. On Epic-Kitchens-100, its SC and BC are 0.9506 and 0.9555, compared with 0.8923 and 0.9223 for TesserAct, and its Cap.Sim is 0.4010, compared with 0.3710 for the next-best method, VIST3A. TesserAct remains competitive on individual appearance metrics, such as image quality on HoiGen and RLBench, aesthetic quality on Dynamic Replica, and motion smoothness on Epic-Kitchens-100. VIST3A also leads in aesthetic quality on Epic-Kitchens-100. These results indicate strong visual consistency across benchmarks, while individual appearance and caption-alignment metrics favor different methods. The depth and reconstruction columns show the value of reading geometry from the same latent future. PLAN4D obtains the best depth metrics on all five datasets, with substantially lower AbsRel and higher threshold accuracy than TesserAct and Gen3R. On Epic-Kitchens-100, it obtains an AbsRel of 0.0766 with δ1 = 0.9265 and δ2 = 0.9846. It also gives the best Chamfer-L1 reconstruction on Epic-Kitchens-100, Dynamic Replica, PointOdyssey, and RLBench among methods with reported reconstruction outputs. On Epic-Kitchens-100, its Chamfer-L1 of 0.2321 is lower than Gen3Rs 0.3390, TesserActs 1.3321, and VIST3As 6.4722. Gen3R is strongest on HoiGen Chamfer-L1, 32 Table 9: Comparison with video-only generation followed by post hoc geometry reconstruction on HoiGen under the main action-conditioned evaluation protocol. Geometric references are reconstructed by applying DA3 to the ground-truth videos. Arrows indicate the preferred direction, and the best value in each column is in bold. Method Subj. Cons. BG Cons. Depth AbsRel Depth δ1 Camera RPE-R Cosmos-3-Nano + VGGT-Omega LongCat-Video + DA3 PLAN4D (Ours) 0.8760 0.8864 0.9035 0.9213 0.9235 0.9334 0.4547 0.2815 0.1125 0.5850 0.6875 0. 0.2933 0.3450 0.1240 but its depth and camera metrics are much worse on the same benchmark. This indicates that lower point-cloud distance in one setting does not necessarily imply temporally coherent RGB-D world model. By contrast, PLAN4D keeps depth and reconstruction strong across scene types, from hand-object interaction to dynamic stereo and robot manipulation. Camera estimation further separates the methods that preserve global 4D structure from those that only recover local geometry. PLAN4D achieves the best reported RPE-R on HoiGen, Dynamic Replica, and PointOdyssey, and matches or approaches perfect relative-rotation accuracy on Dynamic Replica and PointOdyssey. On Epic-Kitchens-100, it achieves RRA@10 and RRA@5 of 1.0000, although TesserAct has lower RPE-R of 0.0946 compared with our 0.1568. TesserAct also leads on the RLBench camera metrics. Gen3R consistently has much larger rotation errors, which reflects the difficulty of maintaining stable global camera motion when geometry is generated without the same latent-level coupling to the video model. The Epic-Kitchens-100 results provide quantitative evidence of visual, geometric, and camera consistency on in-the-wild interactions and, together with HoiGen, support the generality of PLAN4D across two real-world human-object interaction benchmarks. Overall, the full table supports the same conclusion as the main paper: PLAN4D balances action-conditioned video quality, dense geometry, and camera stability in one forward generation process. These quantitative scores complement the qualitative snapshots in the paper, while full qualitative videos remain useful for inspecting the temporal behavior of generated 4D scenes. I.1 Video-Only World Models with Post Hoc Geometry Reconstruction This comparison tests whether strong video-only world model followed by an independent geometry reconstructor can match joint video and 4D generation. We evaluate two additional baselines on HoiGen, including direct combination of the two pretrained backbones used by PLAN4D. Evaluation setting. We use the same 200 HoiGen test examples and action-conditioned generation protocol as the main comparison in Section 4.1 and table 8. Each method receives the initial RGB frame and an action description. For geometric evaluation, we feed the ground-truth video into DA3 and use its reconstructed depth and camera poses as the common reference. The geometric scores therefore measure agreement with DA3-derived pseudo ground truth. We report subject consistency and background consistency for video quality, depth AbsRel and δ1 for depth accuracy, and camera relative rotation error (RPE-R). Depth uses the same per-clip scale-shift alignment as the main evaluation, and camera evaluation follows the same pose-alignment protocol described in Section B. Higher consistency scores and δ1 are better, while lower AbsRel and RPE-R are better. Baseline construction. Cosmos-3-Nano + VGGT-Omega uses Cosmos-3-Nano [1] to generate RGB video and applies VGGT-Omega [93] to reconstruct geometry from the generated frames. This baseline tests post hoc geometry recovery from strong video-only world model. LongCat-Video + DA3 first generates an RGB video with LongCat-Video and then applies DA3 directly to the generated frames. It combines our two pretrained backbones without joint training and tests whether their independent use is sufficient for consistent 4D generation. In both baselines, geometric reconstruction takes place after RGB video generation. Results and analysis. Table 9 shows that PLAN4D achieves the best result on all five reported metrics. Compared with LongCat-Video + DA3, subject and background consistency increase from 0.8864 and 0.9235 to 0.9035 and 0.9334. Depth AbsRel decreases from 0.2815 to 0.1125, depth δ1 increases from 0.6875 to 0.8540, and camera RPE-R decreases from 0.3450 to 0.1240. The 33 Figure 9: Qualitative results of PLAN4D. We provide the model with an initial frame and descriptive text prompt: Removes the red cap from the squeeze bottle. Holds the bottle with both hands. Squeezes the bottle. Drizzles the sauce over the takoyaki in controlled pattern. Finishes adding the sauce. Based on these inputs, PLAN4D generates dense 4D prediction. The figure visualizes the synthesized RGB frames (top row), depth maps (middle row), and 4D global point clouds (bottom row). comparison with Cosmos-3-Nano + VGGT-Omega shows the same advantage across video, depth, and camera metrics. These results illustrate limitation of post hoc geometry recovery. video generator trained only with appearance objectives receives no explicit supervision on the geometry, camera motion, or scene dynamics of its generated future. downstream reconstructor must infer these quantities from the generated images, so visual inconsistencies can propagate into the recovered geometry. In PLAN4D, appearance, depth, camera geometry, and scene flow supervise shared latent representation during joint training. The resulting latent future must support both RGB generation and geometric readout, encouraging visual and 4D consistency within the same rollout. Our stitching framework makes this supervision practical by connecting large-scale video data to pretrained geometry model, while paired dynamic 3D datasets provide additional supervision where available. I.2 More Qualitative Results We provide additional qualitative examples to further evaluate the behavior of PLAN4D across diverse action scenarios. Each example is conditioned on single initial frame and natural-language description, from which the model predicts an evolving 4D future. We visualize the generated RGB frames, depth maps, and global point clouds from the same prediction, allowing appearance, geometry, and temporal consistency to be inspected jointly. The examples cover object manipulation, human motion, physical interaction, and multi-entity indoor dynamics, showing that PLAN4D can produce action-aligned visual changes while preserving coherent 3D structure over time. I.3 Diagnostic Study on ImageText Misalignment Action-conditioned 4D generation assumes that the input frame and the text prompt describe compatible scene. In practice, the two conditions may conflict, and it is important to understand which condition PLAN4D follows in that case. No established benchmark currently evaluates imagetext conflicts for action-conditioned 4D generation, so we conduct targeted diagnostic study. Setting. We select 34 held-out imagetext pairs and keep each original input frame fixed. For each frame, we construct two mismatched prompts, which yields 68 rollouts in total. The two prompt types probe different degrees of conflict. Figure 10: Qualitative results of PLAN4D. We provide the model with an initial frame and descriptive text prompt: Person bends forward, arms extended, performing slow motion movement on the yellow rug. Based on these inputs, PLAN4D generates dense 4D prediction. The figure visualizes the synthesized RGB frames (top row), depth maps (middle row), and 4D global point clouds (bottom row). Figure 11: Qualitative results of PLAN4D. We provide the model with an initial frame and descriptive text prompt: Delivers series of punches to the heavy bag. The bag swings backward / recoils away upon impact. Based on these inputs, PLAN4D generates dense 4D prediction. The figure visualizes the synthesized RGB frames (top row), depth maps (middle row), and 4D global point clouds (bottom row). Type A, semantically disjoint. The prompt describes an event that cannot occur in the observed scene. For example, an egocentric kitchen frame showing hand on dough is paired with group of penguins dives from an iceberg into the cold ocean. Type B, scene editing. The prompt requests an implausible transformation of the observed scene, such as Transform the dough into pile of transparent glass marbles and make the dark counter become rippling beach sand. 35 Figure 12: Qualitative results of PLAN4D. We provide the model with an initial frame and descriptive text prompt: Man lifts leg, monkey stands and walks, cow shifts position in room. Based on these inputs, PLAN4D generates dense 4D prediction. The figure visualizes the synthesized RGB frames (top row), depth maps (middle row), and 4D global point clouds (bottom row). Table 10: Diagnostic study on imagetext misalignment. Each of the 34 held-out input frames is paired with one semantically disjoint prompt (Type A) and one scene-editing prompt (Type B), giving 68 rollouts. Each entry counts the rollouts manually assigned to an outcome. denotes satisfying the prompt through scene cut, denotes satisfying it through an instantaneous morph, and denotes preserving the original scene and continuing plausible action. Each row sums to = 34. Mismatch type C: cut M: morph P: plausible Type A: semantically disjoint (n = 34) Type B: scene editing (n = 34) 34 0 30 0 4 Categorization protocol. We manually assign each rollout to one of three outcomes. (cut) denotes rollout that satisfies the prompt through scene cut to the described content. (morph) denotes rollout that satisfies the prompt through an instantaneous transformation of objects or surfaces in the observed scene. (plausible) denotes rollout that preserves the original scene and continues plausible action instead of realizing the conflicting prompt. Results. Table 10 summarizes the outcomes. For Type A, all 34 rollouts begin by preserving the input scene and then transition to the scene described by the prompt, in manner reminiscent of cinematic montage cut. For Type B, 30 of the 34 rollouts introduce the requested objects through abrupt transformations, while the remaining 4 preserve the original scene and continue plausible action. Qualitative examples and input prompts. Figure 13 illustrates the three outcomes with four selected rollouts. We show the initial image and sample the generated RGB and depth at 0.5, 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5 seconds. The input text prompts are: (a) Scene transition. violinist performs alone under spotlight in an empty concert hall. (b) Object morph. Keep the same man, pose, and restaurant background, but transform the pizza in his hands into large bouquet of yellow sunflowers and make his black shirt turn bright red. (c) Scene morph. Keep the same man, pose, lawn, and modern building, but transform the camera stabilizer into an open yellow umbrella and turn the grass beneath him into shallow reflective water. 36 Figure 13: Qualitative outcomes under imagetext misalignment. Each case shows RGB above the corresponding predicted depth at seven shared time points. The first RGB column is the conditioning image. Case (a) illustrates scene transition (C) under Type A. Cases (b) and (c) illustrate object and scene transformations (M) under Type B. Case (d) preserves the original scene and continues plausible action (P) under Type B. The complete input prompts are reported in the text. (d) Plausible continuation. Keep the same people, bowl, and tabletop, but make every blueberry disappear and fill the white bowl with shiny gold coins as the container is tilted above it. In (a), the egocentric kitchen view gives way to close-up of violinist. In (b), sunflower bouquet replaces the pizza while the person and restaurant remain recognizable. In (c), an umbrella appears in place of the stabilizer and the lawn develops reflective water surface. In (d), the model continues pouring blueberries into the bowl without introducing the requested gold coins. The paired depth maps follow the main foreground boundaries in the displayed frames, including the violinist, expanding bouquet, umbrella, and hands around the bowl. This correspondence can coexist with an implausible scene change or incomplete prompt fulfillment, as also illustrated by the unchanged black shirt in (b). The snapshots provide qualitative evidence of agreement between RGB and predicted depth, while physical continuity and complete adherence to the conflicting prompt remain separate properties. Analysis. The diagnostic results in Table 10 and fig. 13 show that PLAN4D generally prioritizes the text condition when the image and text conflict. When the prompt cannot be naturally realized in the observed scene, the model resolves the mismatch through scene transition or an instantaneous transformation. This behavior mainly originates from the text-conditioned video prior. The stitched geometry decoder still produces synchronized depth, camera rays, and scene flow for the generated trajectory, although physical continuity may be broken at the transition. Because PLAN4D explicitly predicts geometry such as scene flow and camera rays, these abrupt transitions may also be detectable as geometric discontinuities. Such discontinuities could provide lightweight infeasibility signal for downstream planning.

sections.title: NeurIPS Paper Checklist
sections.content: 1. Claims Question: Do the main claims made in the abstract and introduction accurately reflect the papers contributions and scope? Answer: [Yes] Justification: The Abstract and Sec. 1 state the main contributions and scope clearly, and these claims are supported by the experimental evidence summarized in Sec. 4. Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that the abstract and introduction do not include the claims made in the paper. The abstract and/or introduction should clearly state the claims made, including the contributions made in the paper and important assumptions and limitations. [No] or [N/A] answer to this question will not be perceived well by the reviewers. The claims made should match theoretical and experimental results, and reflect how much the results can be expected to generalize to other settings. It is fine to include aspirational goals as motivation as long as it is clear that these goals are not attained by the paper. 2. Limitations Question: Does the paper discuss the limitations of the work performed by the authors? Answer: [Yes] Justification: The manuscript now discusses the main limitations explicitly in Sec. D, including that the current model does not directly output executable actions and has not yet been validated as full closed-loop embodied system. Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that the paper has no limitation while the answer [No] means that the paper has limitations, but those are not discussed in the paper. The authors are encouraged to create separate Limitations section in their paper. The paper should point out any strong assumptions and how robust the results are to violations of these assumptions (e.g., independence assumptions, noiseless settings, model well-specification, asymptotic approximations only holding locally). The authors should reflect on how these assumptions might be violated in practice and what the implications would be. The authors should reflect on the scope of the claims made, e.g., if the approach was only tested on few datasets or with few runs. In general, empirical results often depend on implicit assumptions, which should be articulated. The authors should reflect on the factors that influence the performance of the approach. For example, facial recognition algorithm may perform poorly when image resolution is low or images are taken in low lighting. Or speech-to-text system might not be used reliably to provide closed captions for online lectures because it fails to handle technical jargon. The authors should discuss the computational efficiency of the proposed algorithms and how they scale with dataset size. If applicable, the authors should discuss possible limitations of their approach to address problems of privacy and fairness. While the authors might fear that complete honesty about limitations might be used by reviewers as grounds for rejection, worse outcome might be that reviewers discover limitations that arent acknowledged in the paper. The authors should use their best judgment and recognize that individual actions in favor of transparency play an important role in developing norms that preserve the integrity of the community. Reviewers will be specifically instructed to not penalize honesty concerning limitations. 3. Theory assumptions and proofs Question: For each theoretical result, does the paper provide the full set of assumptions and complete (and correct) proof? Answer: [N/A] Justification: The paper does not present theorem-style theoretical results or formal proofs. Its mathematical content defines the model, losses, and evaluation setup in Sec. 3 and the Appendix. Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include theoretical results. All the theorems, formulas, and proofs in the paper should be numbered and crossreferenced. All assumptions should be clearly stated or referenced in the statement of any theorems. The proofs can either appear in the main paper or the supplemental material, but if they appear in the supplemental material, the authors are encouraged to provide short proof sketch to provide intuition. Inversely, any informal proof provided in the core of the paper should be complemented by formal proofs provided in appendix or supplemental material. Theorems and Lemmas that the proof relies upon should be properly referenced. 4. Experimental result reproducibility Question: Does the paper fully disclose all the information needed to reproduce the main experimental results of the paper to the extent that it affects the main claims and/or conclusions of the paper (regardless of whether the code and data are provided or not)? Answer: [Yes] Justification: Sec. 3, Sec. 4, and Sec. describe the architecture, staged training pipeline, losses, datasets, and evaluation protocols that underpin the main results. Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments. If the paper includes experiments, [No] answer to this question will not be perceived well by the reviewers: Making the paper reproducible is important, regardless of whether the code and data are provided or not. If the contribution is dataset and/or model, the authors should describe the steps taken to make their results reproducible or verifiable. Depending on the contribution, reproducibility can be accomplished in various ways. For example, if the contribution is novel architecture, describing the architecture fully might suffice, or if the contribution is specific model and empirical evaluation, it may be necessary to either make it possible for others to replicate the model with the same dataset, or provide access to the model. In general. releasing code and data is often one good way to accomplish this, but reproducibility can also be provided via detailed instructions for how to replicate the results, access to hosted model (e.g., in the case of large language model), releasing of model checkpoint, or other means that are appropriate to the research performed. While NeurIPS does not require releasing code, the conference does require all submissions to provide some reasonable avenue for reproducibility, which may depend on the nature of the contribution. For example (a) If the contribution is primarily new algorithm, the paper should make it clear how to reproduce that algorithm. (b) If the contribution is primarily new model architecture, the paper should describe the architecture clearly and fully. (c) If the contribution is new model (e.g., large language model), then there should either be way to access this model for reproducing the results or way to reproduce the model (e.g., with an open-source dataset or instructions for how to construct the dataset). (d) We recognize that reproducibility may be tricky in some cases, in which case authors are welcome to describe the particular way they provide for reproducibility. In the case of closed-source models, it may be that access to the model is limited in some way (e.g., to registered users), but it should be possible for other researchers to have some path to reproducing or verifying the results. 39 5. Open access to data and code Question: Does the paper provide open access to the data and code, with sufficient instructions to faithfully reproduce the main experimental results, as described in supplemental material? Answer: [Yes] Justification: This paper relies entirely on open-source data, and the code will be made available upon acceptance. Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that paper does not include experiments requiring code. Please see the NeurIPS code and data submission guidelines (https://neurips.cc/ public/guides/CodeSubmissionPolicy) for more details. While we encourage the release of code and data, we understand that this might not be possible, so [No] is an acceptable answer. Papers cannot be rejected simply for not including code, unless this is central to the contribution (e.g., for new open-source benchmark). The instructions should contain the exact command and environment needed to run to reproduce the results. See the NeurIPS code and data submission guidelines (https: //neurips.cc/public/guides/CodeSubmissionPolicy) for more details. The authors should provide instructions on data access and preparation, including how to access the raw data, preprocessed data, intermediate data, and generated data, etc. The authors should provide scripts to reproduce all experimental results for the new proposed method and baselines. If only subset of experiments are reproducible, they should state which ones are omitted from the script and why. At submission time, to preserve anonymity, the authors should release anonymized versions (if applicable). Providing as much information as possible in supplemental material (appended to the paper) is recommended, but including URLs to data and code is permitted. 6. Experimental setting/details Question: Does the paper specify all the training and test details (e.g., data splits, hyperparameters, how they were chosen, type of optimizer) necessary to understand the results? Answer: [Yes] Justification: Sec. 4 specifies the training stages, datasets, evaluation benchmarks, clip lengths, and hardware scale, while Sec. details the supervision sources and loss formulations needed to interpret the reported results. Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments. The experimental setting should be presented in the core of the paper to level of detail that is necessary to appreciate the results and make sense of them. The full details can be provided either with the code, in appendix, or as supplemental material. 7. Experiment statistical significance Question: Does the paper report error bars suitably and correctly defined or other appropriate information about the statistical significance of the experiments? Answer: [Yes] Justification: Experimental results are tested multiple times to ensure stability and reliability. Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments. The authors should answer [Yes] if the results are accompanied by error bars, confidence intervals, or statistical significance tests, at least for the experiments that support the main claims of the paper. 40 The factors of variability that the error bars are capturing should be clearly stated (for example, train/test split, initialization, random drawing of some parameter, or overall run with given experimental conditions). The method for calculating the error bars should be explained (closed form formula, call to library function, bootstrap, etc.) The assumptions made should be given (e.g., Normally distributed errors). It should be clear whether the error bar is the standard deviation or the standard error of the mean. It is OK to report 1-sigma error bars, but one should state it. The authors should preferably report 2-sigma error bar than state that they have 96% CI, if the hypothesis of Normality of errors is not verified. For asymmetric distributions, the authors should be careful not to show in tables or figures symmetric error bars that would yield results that are out of range (e.g., negative error rates). If error bars are reported in tables or plots, the authors should explain in the text how they were calculated and reference the corresponding figures or tables in the text. 8. Experiments compute resources Question: For each experiment, does the paper provide sufficient information on the computer resources (type of compute workers, memory, time of execution) needed to reproduce the experiments? Answer: [Yes] Justification: Sec. 4 reports GPU types, GPU counts, batch size, and training epochs for the three stages. Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments. The paper should indicate the type of compute workers CPU or GPU, internal cluster, or cloud provider, including relevant memory and storage. The paper should provide the amount of compute required for each of the individual experimental runs as well as estimate the total compute. The paper should disclose whether the full research project required more compute than the experiments reported in the paper (e.g., preliminary or failed experiments that didnt make it into the paper). 9. Code of ethics Question: Does the research conducted in the paper conform, in every respect, with the NeurIPS Code of Ethics https://neurips.cc/public/EthicsGuidelines? Answer: [Yes] Justification: Yes. The study is an algorithmic evaluation on existing datasets and pretrained models, it does not involve human subjects, and we are not aware of any aspect of the work that departs from the NeurIPS Code of Ethics. Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that the authors have not reviewed the NeurIPS Code of Ethics. If the authors answer [No], they should explain the special circumstances that require deviation from the Code of Ethics. The authors should make sure to preserve anonymity (e.g., if there is special consideration due to laws or regulations in their jurisdiction). 10. Broader impacts Question: Does the paper discuss both potential positive societal impacts and negative societal impacts of the work performed? Answer: [Yes] 41 Justification: Sec. discusses both positive uses for embodied planning and simulation and possible negative impacts such as surveillance, overreliance on incorrect predictions, and misuse in safety-critical settings, together with mitigation considerations. Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that there is no societal impact of the work performed. If the authors answer [N/A] or [No], they should explain why their work has no societal impact or why the paper does not address societal impact. Examples of negative societal impacts include potential malicious or unintended uses (e.g., disinformation, generating fake profiles, surveillance), fairness considerations (e.g., deployment of technologies that could make decisions that unfairly impact specific groups), privacy considerations, and security considerations. The conference expects that many papers will be foundational research and not tied to particular applications, let alone deployments. However, if there is direct path to any negative applications, the authors should point it out. For example, it is legitimate to point out that an improvement in the quality of generative models could be used to generate Deepfakes for disinformation. On the other hand, it is not needed to point out that generic algorithm for optimizing neural networks could enable people to train models that generate Deepfakes faster. The authors should consider possible harms that could arise when the technology is being used as intended and functioning correctly, harms that could arise when the technology is being used as intended but gives incorrect results, and harms following from (intentional or unintentional) misuse of the technology. If there are negative societal impacts, the authors could also discuss possible mitigation strategies (e.g., gated release of models, providing defenses in addition to attacks, mechanisms for monitoring misuse, mechanisms to monitor how system learns from feedback over time, improving the efficiency and accessibility of ML). 11. Safeguards Question: Does the paper describe safeguards that have been put in place for responsible release of data or models that have high risk for misuse (e.g., pre-trained language models, image generators, or scraped datasets)? Answer: [N/A] Justification: This submission poses no such risks. Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that the paper poses no such risks. Released models that have high risk for misuse or dual-use should be released with necessary safeguards to allow for controlled use of the model, for example by requiring that users adhere to usage guidelines or restrictions to access the model or implementing safety filters. Datasets that have been scraped from the Internet could pose safety risks. The authors should describe how they avoided releasing unsafe images. We recognize that providing effective safeguards is challenging, and many papers do not require this, but we encourage authors to take this into account and make best faith effort. 12. Licenses for existing assets Question: Are the creators or original owners of assets (e.g., code, data, models), used in the paper, properly credited and are the license and terms of use explicitly mentioned and properly respected? Answer: [Yes] Justification: The manuscript now summarizes the external code, model, and dataset assets together with their licenses or usage terms in Sec. F, and the main paper cites the original creators of the assets used in training, evaluation, and comparison.
